query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended as energetic structural materials, what single testable hypothesis identifies an intervention that could improve ductility and uniform deformability without sacrificing high strength or impact-induced energy release? State the proposed intervention, its hypothesized mechanism, the improvement expected relative to the untreated baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and a decisive experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small content of interstitial oxygen (~0.5 at.%) to a fully recrystallized, fine‐grained FCC refractory high-entropy alloy (such as a CoCrNiV-type alloy) will enhance uniform ductility by modestly increasing the stacking fault energy and promoting dislocation glide, without compromising its high yield strength or the material’s capacity for impact-induced energy release.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase, fully recrystallized fine‐grained FCC refractory high-entropy alloy (e.g., CoCrNiV alloy processed by cold rolling and appropriate heat treatment) exhibiting high yield strength and high impact energy release.
generation.intervention: Incorporation of a low concentration (around 0.5 atomic percent) of interstitial oxygen into the alloy during processing.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature quasi-static tensile loading and high strain-rate (impact) conditions; processing conditions similar to those used to achieve a fully recrystallized fine-grained microstructure.
generation.structural_mediator: A slight lattice distortion and an increase in stacking fault energy due to segregated oxygen atoms that occupy interstitial sites, resulting in enhanced dislocation mobility and stabilized dislocation and stacking fault structures.
generation.mechanism: Interstitial oxygen atoms produce modest lattice distortion without forming detrimental oxide precipitates. This perturbation increases the stacking fault energy in a controlled fashion that favors a persistent dislocation glide mechanism, thereby boosting strain hardening and uniform ductility while maintaining the solid solution strengthening that underpins high yield strength and impact energy release.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated alloy, the oxygen-doped alloy is expected to show a measurable increase in uniform elongation (improved ductility) while retaining similar levels of high yield strength and impact-induced energy absorption.
generation.baseline: The untreated refractory high-entropy alloy with a fully recrystallized fine-grained FCC structure exhibiting high yield strength (~1060 MPa) with good energy release characteristics.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect should hold only for low oxygen contents (e.g., ≤0.5 at.%) that avoid the formation of oxide precipitates or embrittlement; higher oxygen levels may compromise phase stability and mechanical properties.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal oxygen concentration and its precise influence on stacking fault energy and dislocation behavior under dynamic loading conditions need further quantitative evaluation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of refractory high-entropy alloy samples with identical base composition and processing to obtain a fully recrystallized fine-grained FCC structure. One set is left untreated (control) and the other is doped with ~0.5 at.% interstitial oxygen during alloy processing. Characterize the microstructure (grain size, dislocation density, stacking fault characteristics) via SEM/TEM. Conduct room-temperature tensile tests and high strain-rate impact tests on both sets.
measurements: Tensile stress–strain curves (to determine yield strength and uniform elongation)
Impact tests measuring energy absorption or energy release characteristics
Microstructure analysis (grain size, stacking fault density, and dislocation patterns)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the oxygen-doped samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in uniform elongation (ductility) compared to the control, or if there is any detrimental reduction in yield strength or impact-induced energy release compared to the untreated alloy.

cited_evidence.text: Fully recrystallized FG Co33Cr24Ni33V10 alloys, CR750 and CR800, were produced by cold rolling at room temperature and heat treatment. By conducting tensile tests and microstructure characterization, the main conclusions can be summarized as follows: The Co33Cr24Ni33V10 alloy maintained a single-phase FCC structure and exhibited superior phase stability throughout the processes of rolling, heat treatment, and tensile deformation. The primary deformation mechanisms of the CR750 and CR800 alloys were dislocation slip and SFs, with no occurrence of twinning or phase transformation. The fully recrystallized FG structure of CR750 alloy with the minimum mean grain size of 0.95 μm exhibited a high yield strength of 1060 MPa and a uniform elongation of 24.1%. The exceptional strength can be attributed to the presence of the FG structure and solid solution strengthening effect, while the remarkable ductility arises from the excellent strain-hardening ability primarily governed by dislocations and SFs.

This study employed first-principles calculations combined with the Special Quasi-random Structure (SQS) technique to systematically investigate the effects of interstitial elements C, N, and O on the structural, electronic, and mechanical properties of NiCoCr medium-entropy alloys (MEAs). The key findings are summarized as follows: Interstitial site preference and lattice distortion: C and N preferentially occupy octahedral interstitial sites, while O exhibits a higher diffusion rate between octahedral and tetrahedral sites, effectively alleviating stress concentration. The dissolution of these interstitial atoms causes significant lattice distortion, with O causing the most noticeable distortion (16.82%), followed by N (10.84%) and C (9.27%). Mechanical properties: The introduction of interstitial atoms increases the elastic constants and SFE, indicating an improvement in stiffness and resistance to plastic deformation. O doping leads to the most significant increase in SFE (69 mJ/m2, from −35 mJ/m2 to 34 mJ/m2), followed by N (58 mJ/m2) and C (54 mJ/m2). It optimizes the strength–ductility balance of the alloy by suppressing twinning and promoting dislocation glide. Electronic i
